title: The Hotel Corridor: William James, the Sick Years, and the Right to Believe
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Astor House, Broadway at Vesey Street: the first son
stops.date_confidence: attested: born 11 January 1842 at the Astor House. The coordinate is the hotel site at 225 Broadway, not the generic New York centroid that circulates in the dossier
stops.campa: In a suite at the Astor House, the Broadway hotel at Vesey Street where his parents are lodging between homes, Mary Walsh James gives birth to a first son. He is named William, after the grandfather whose Albany fortune pays for everything that follows: the tutors, the crossings, the years of no fixed address. Henry James Sr. has no profession and no intention of acquiring one. A second son, Henry, arrives the next year in the same city. The family will not own a house of its own until William is a middle-aged professor.
suggested_refs: The Astor House at 225 Broadway, demolished in stages between 1913 and 1926

stops.name: Windsor, England: the father's vastation
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1844 for the vastation, which Wikipedia places at Windsor; the day is a placeholder. The Piccadilly lodgings named in the dossier for these years are not supported by any fetched source and are dropped here
stops.campa: The family is living in England when Henry James Sr., sitting at table after dinner, is seized by a formless terror he later calls a vastation: a squatting shape in the room, radiating fear, and no cause for it anywhere. He is two years recovering. What he finds at the end of the two years is Emanuel Swedenborg, dead seventy years, whose correspondences between the natural world and the spiritual become the weather of the house his sons grow up in. The question of what a state like that is, and what it is evidence of, stays open in the house and in the son's work after it. William is two years old.
suggested_refs: Henry James Sr.'s Swedenborgian writings, the theological weather of the household
The Swedenborgian current the sons were raised inside and each refused differently

stops.name: Paris: the sensuous education
stops.date_confidence: year approximate: the Stanford Encyclopedia gives 1855-1858 for the European span without resolving which city held the family in which months; the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: Between Geneva and Boulogne the household lands in Paris, where the boys are put to languages and drawing under whatever tutor their father has most recently approved of and will shortly dismiss. Henry Sr. calls this a sensuous education and means it against the American schoolroom and against any fixed curriculum. What the children come away with is French, German, the galleries, and the habit of arriving somewhere new. None of them is being trained for a trade. William is fourteen and draws better than anyone else in the family.
suggested_refs: Henry James Sr.'s program of an education without school, curriculum, or country

stops.name: Boulogne-sur-Mer, No. 20 Rue Neuve Chaussee
stops.date_confidence: attested to the summer of 1857 with the street address; the family had crossed to Newport by 1858, so the dossier's range of 1857-1859 overshoots by a year
stops.campa: In the summer the household sets up at No. 20 Rue Neuve Chaussee in the Channel port, within sight of the boats that carry them back and forth. It is the fourth country in three years. William works at the local college and reads chemistry on his own; his brother Henry falls ill. Their father, whose income arrives from Albany without his doing anything to earn it, is running out of Europe to try. By the following year the family has crossed and is at Newport.
suggested_refs: The James household at No. 20 Rue Neuve Chaussee, Boulogne-sur-Mer, summer 1857

stops.name: Geneva: the Academy
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1859-1860 by the Stanford Encyclopedia timeline; the month is a placeholder. This second Geneva residence follows a brief 1858 stay at Newport and precedes the return to Newport in 1860
stops.campa: The family has been at Newport for a year and Henry Sr. has changed his mind about American schooling again, so they cross east once more. At the Academy of Geneva, the closest thing to an institution the father's program has yet permitted, William enrols in the scientific section and does well. Anatomy, chemistry, mathematics; a lecture hall instead of a tutor's parlour. He is seventeen and for the first time is being measured against other students by people who are not his father. The record of these two Swiss years is thin.
suggested_refs: The Academy of Geneva, scientific section, 1859-1860

stops.name: Bonn: the last European summer
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Wikipedia places Bonn inside the 1855-1860 circuit and dates the return to Newport to 1860, which puts the Bonn stay in the summer of 1860. The dossier's 1859 belongs to Geneva instead; the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: The last stop before the Atlantic is Bonn, where the boys are boarded with German families to fix the language. William writes home in a mixture of tongues and argues with his father by post about painting, and he wins the argument: Henry Sr. has decided the family will go back to Newport so that his eldest can study with a painter. The German taken away from this summer gets used seven years later, in a sickroom, reading Helmholtz and Fechner and hunting for a physiology of the mind.
suggested_refs: The German boarding arrangements at Bonn, summer 1860

stops.name: Newport: the studio of William Morris Hunt
stops.date_confidence: corrected: the Hunt apprenticeship belongs to the second Newport residence, 1860-61, not to the 1858 stay, which the dossier welds it to. The month is a placeholder and the studio's exact address is not established, so the Newport town coordinate stands in
stops.campa: William Morris Hunt keeps pupils at Newport, and William James is one of them for a year. He draws well; everyone who sees the sheets says so, and some of the sheets survive. Then, in 1861, he stops. The reasons given afterwards vary with the teller: the father's pressure, the son's own verdict on his talent, the pull of chemistry. The version in which Henry Sr. simply forbids a painter's life is the tidiest of them and the least supported by anything written at the time. The date is certain. The reason is not, and no source reached here settles it.
suggested_refs: Surviving drawings and studies from James's year with William Morris Hunt, 1860-61

segments.name: Chemistry, the Museum, and the River

stops.name: Lawrence Scientific School, Harvard: the brush put down
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1861 for entry; the month marks the academic year. The coordinate is the Harvard Yard pin already used elsewhere for Harvard-set stops
stops.campa: He enters the Lawrence Scientific School in the autumn of 1861 to read chemistry, and the brush is put down and stays down. He works at the bench, complains of the smells and the arithmetic, and within two years has shifted across to comparative anatomy, which suits him better because it is looked at rather than calculated. The country is at war the entire time he is there. Two of his younger brothers, Wilky and Bob, enlist. William stays at the bench in Cambridge, kept there by his father's Albany money.
suggested_refs: The Lawrence Scientific School, Harvard's engineering and science annex until 1906

stops.name: Museum of Comparative Zoology: under Agassiz
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: James's work under Louis Agassiz at the museum spans roughly 1861 to 1865 and is not dated more precisely in any fetched source; the year and month order the segment
stops.campa: Louis Agassiz has built a museum of specimens at Harvard and rules it absolutely. James works under him and takes from him a discipline he never afterwards gives up: look at the thing itself, count it, draw it, do not take the textbook's word for it. He also watches Agassiz refuse Darwin outright and defend the separate creation of the human races, and takes a second lesson from that, which is that a great observer can be wrong at the top of his voice. Both lessons are in the Principles thirty years later.
suggested_refs: The Museum of Comparative Zoology, founded by Agassiz in 1859

stops.name: Harvard Medical School, North Grove Street
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1864 for the start of medical study; the month is a placeholder. The coordinate is the Nominatim location of North Grove Street in Boston's West End, about 255 metres from the value carried in the dossier
stops.campa: He begins medicine at the Grove Street building in Boston's West End, the school's home since 1847, chosen less because he wants to practise than because it is the one scientific career a man can be paid for. The course takes him five years instead of three. Illness interrupts it twice: a year in Brazil, then eighteen months in Germany. His back hurts constantly, his eyes fail under any long reading, and he writes to his cousins about wanting to be dead.
suggested_refs: The Harvard Medical School building on North Grove Street, occupied 1847-1883

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro: the Thayer Expedition lands
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Thayer Expedition's Brazilian year is documented, but the April-May dating of the Rio stay comes from the dossier and the Harvard revista article and was not independently pinned to a month
stops.campa: Agassiz takes a party to Brazil to collect fish and, he hopes, to disprove Darwin with them. James goes along as a volunteer collector at his own expense. The party lands at Rio, is received by the imperial court and by coffee planters in the hills, and James, twenty-three and never outside Europe and New England before, writes home about the enslaved men who carry the baggage and about how little he understands of anything in front of him. Then he comes down with what the party calls varioloid, a mild smallpox, and spends weeks in a darkened room.
suggested_refs: The Thayer Expedition of 1865-66, financed by Nathaniel Thayer to collect Amazonian fish

stops.name: The upper Amazon: eight months and out
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the ascent of the Amazon in 1865 is documented, but the specific stretch near Tefe and the month are dossier claims that no fetched source confirms
stops.campa: Recovered, he goes up the river anyway, collecting fish along the reaches above Manaus, packing barrels, keeping a notebook, sketching what comes up in the nets. He is good at the work and hates it. The seasickness never lifts, the science is another man's carried out by other men's hands, and he writes home that he was not made to be a naturalist in the field. Eight months after landing in Brazil he leaves the expedition and turns north for home.
suggested_refs: James's Brazilian field notebooks and sketches, Houghton Library

segments.name: Germany, the Degree, and the Bottom

stops.name: Dresden: reading the new physiology
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1867-1868 German period; the month and the order of cities within that period are approximate
stops.campa: Medical study breaks down again and he sails for Germany, nominally for the baths and the back, actually because Germany is where the new physiology is being made. In Dresden he reads Helmholtz on the eye and Fechner on the measurement of sensation, and finds the proposition he will not let go of afterwards: that states of mind might be counted. He is twenty-five, unemployed, dependent on his father's money, and in pain most days. The letters home from these months catalogue his own symptoms with a physiologist's precision and no idea what to do about them.
suggested_refs: Fechner's Elemente der Psychophysik (1860) and Helmholtz's Handbuch der physiologischen Optik (1867)

stops.name: Berlin: physiology lectures and the waters at Teplitz
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1867-1868 German period, which included Dresden, Bad Teplitz and Berlin; the month is a placeholder and the sequence within the period is not fixed by any fetched source
stops.campa: In Berlin he attends physiology lectures at the university and takes the waters at Teplitz between terms, moving from spa to lecture hall on an invalid's schedule. The psychology he is reading about is being built in German laboratories by men with instruments and assistants, and he has neither. What he carries out of the year is a conviction rather than a method: that mental life is continuous with the body and can be studied the way anything else in nature is studied. He sails home in the autumn of 1868 with no degree and no position.
suggested_refs: The Berlin university physiology lectures of 1867-68

stops.name: Harvard Medical School: the M.D. and no practice
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1869; the day is a placeholder
stops.campa: He takes the degree in June, five years after starting it, and never sees a patient. The M.D. is the only credential he will ever hold; every professorship that follows is in a subject he is not certified in. What the training leaves him is a habit of mind rather than a practice, and in the psychology he goes on to write the mind is never anywhere but in a body. When he takes up habit, or emotion, or the will, he takes them up as muscles, breath, the viscera, the set of the jaw.
suggested_refs: James's Harvard M.D., June 1869, never used in practice

stops.name: Quincy Street, Cambridge: the sick years
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the crisis runs roughly from 1869 into the early 1870s with no dated boundaries. The January placeholder orders the segment, and the family's exact Quincy Street address in these months is inferred from standard biography rather than confirmed in a fetched source
stops.campa: For three years he lives in his father's house, twenty-eight years old, qualified for a profession he will not enter, unable to work more than an hour at a stretch. Insomnia, back pain, eye trouble, and a fear he does not name to the family. Thirty years later, in the Gifford Lectures, he prints an account of it as the testimony of an anonymous French correspondent: a young man who sees in memory an epileptic patient, greenish, knees drawn up against his chin, and understands that nothing separates him from that. He gives the young man a nationality and withholds a name. Nobody who knows him is fooled.
suggested_refs: The 'French correspondent' passage in The Varieties of Religious Experience, Lecture VII

stops.name: Quincy Street, Cambridge: the Renouvier entry
stops.date_confidence: attested: the diary entry is dated 30 April 1870 and is printed within the editorial narrative of The Letters of William James, vol. I, rather than reproduced as a facsimile page
stops.campa: He has been reading the second of Charles Renouvier's Essais, and what he finds there is a definition of free will that does not require the universe to cooperate: the sustaining of a thought because I choose to when I might have other thoughts. He writes it into the diary and then writes the sentence that afterwards gets quoted without the rest of the paragraph. The rest is provisional, hedged, and given a term of exactly one year: for the present, until next year, and no further than that. The symptoms do not stop. He is ill on and off for two years more.
stops.quote: I think that yesterday was a crisis in my life. I finished the first part of Renouvier's second "Essais" and see no reason why his definition of Free Will--"the sustaining of a thought because I choose to when I might have other thoughts"--need be the definition of an illusion. At any rate, I will assume for the present--until next year--that it is no illusion. My first act of free will shall be to believe in free will.
stops.quote_source: Diary entry, 30 April 1870, in The Letters of William James, vol. I, ed. Henry James (Boston: Atlantic Monthly Press, 1920)
suggested_refs: Charles Renouvier, Essais de critique generale, second essay
sources: The Letters of William James, vol. I (1920), Project Gutenberg ebook 40307

stops.name: Cambridge: the Metaphysical Club, one year only
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1872: the club existed for a single year, January to December. Its meeting place is not established, so the generic Cambridge coordinate stands in. No record of a club under this name survives outside Charles Peirce's recollections, written decades afterwards
stops.campa: Half a dozen young men in Cambridge meet through 1872 to argue: Charles Sanders Peirce, mathematician and logician; Chauncey Wright, the group's resident skeptic; Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr., lately of the Twentieth Massachusetts; James, not yet employed by anyone. Peirce puts to them a rule for settling disputes about meaning by asking what practical difference a belief would make if it were true. The club lasts a year and leaves no minutes. Everything known about it comes from what its members remembered afterwards, and Peirce wrote his account down thirty-five years late.
suggested_refs: Peirce's later accounts of the Metaphysical Club, the only surviving record of its existence

stops.name: Harvard: the physiology instructorship
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1872-73 for the appointment; the September placeholder marks the academic year
stops.campa: Harvard's president Charles William Eliot offers him an instructorship in physiology and he takes it. It is the first work he has ever been paid for. He is thirty years old and has been kept by his father until this week. He teaches from the blackboard and the specimen table, badly at first, and then not badly. He will hold a Harvard appointment for thirty-five years while its subject changes under him twice, physiology to psychology to philosophy, without his ever holding a degree in either of the last two.
suggested_refs: Charles William Eliot's reconstruction of Harvard, 1869-1909

stops.name: Harvard: the demonstration room
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1875-76 for the course and its demonstration space; the month is a placeholder. The claim that this was the first American psychology laboratory is contested, G. Stanley Hall's later and more formally organized Johns Hopkins laboratory having the better claim
stops.campa: He offers a course called The Relations between Physiology and Psychology and asks the college for a room and a small appropriation for apparatus: chronoscopes, tuning forks, weights for judging the smallest difference a hand can feel. Students come in and are measured. James makes no claim for the room beyond what he wants it for, which is to show a class that a sensation has a duration you can put a number on. Whether that makes it the first psychology laboratory in America depends on what is allowed to count as a laboratory, and the question has never been settled.
suggested_refs: G. Stanley Hall's Johns Hopkins laboratory, the rival claimant to priority
sources: New England Historical Society, 'William James Founds Psychology in America'

stops.name: Boston: a marriage and a contract in one year
stops.date_confidence: the year 1878 is attested for both the marriage and the Holt contract; the day precision of 10 July comes from the dossier alone and could not be independently confirmed. The 'loathsome, distended' phrase is carried from published biography through the dossier and was not re-verified against the letter itself
stops.campa: He marries Alice Howe Gibbens, a Boston schoolteacher, and in the same year signs with the publisher Henry Holt for a textbook of the new psychology, a job the contract allows perhaps two years for. He delivers it in twelve, at some fourteen hundred pages, and calls the thing in private a loathsome, distended, tumefied, bloated, dropsical mass. The invalid years end around here. Alice takes his dictation, reads to him when the eyes fail, runs a household through five children and one small grave, and keeps him at the desk.
suggested_refs: The Henry Holt contract of 1878 and the twelve years it took to satisfy

stops.name: Cambridge: the nitrous oxide experiments
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1882; the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: Benjamin Paul Blood, a farmer and pamphleteer from upstate New York, has published a tract claiming that nitrous oxide opens what he calls an anaesthetic revelation, and James takes him seriously enough to try the gas on himself. Under it the oppositions he has spent his working life inside come apart: yes and no, one and many, the same thing seen from two sides at once. He distrusts the record of it afterwards and keeps the experience anyway. He goes under with a pencil in his hand, and the notes read as gibberish when he sobers up and reads them back.
suggested_refs: Benjamin Paul Blood, The Anaesthetic Revelation and the Gist of Philosophy (1874)

stops.name: Boston: the American Society for Psychical Research founded
stops.date_confidence: corrected: the American Society for Psychical Research was established in December 1884, not 1885 as the dossier has it, with its first meetings in the rooms of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. The day is a placeholder
stops.campa: In rooms lent by the American Academy of Arts and Sciences a society is founded to investigate telepathy, apparitions and trance by the methods used on anything else. Simon Newcomb the astronomer takes the chair. James is one of the vice-presidents, alongside G. Stanley Hall, Edward Pickering and Henry Pickering Bowditch. The premise is that such reports are either true or explicable and that no third option, embarrassed silence, is respectable in a laboratory. He gives twenty-five years to it and is told for twenty-five years that it is beneath him.
suggested_refs: The American Society for Psychical Research, founded December 1884 after William Fletcher Barrett's American visit

stops.name: Boston: Leonora Piper's sitting room
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the sittings begin in 1885 and run for decades; the month is a placeholder. Wikipedia confirms an infant son's death before 1885, but the child's name and dates, Herman James 1884-1885, are dossier-only, and the ordering of the sittings after that death is the dossier's
stops.campa: Their infant son is dead. Alice goes to a Boston housewife who falls into trance and speaks in other voices, and William follows in order to catch her out. He does not catch her out. He puts detectives on her, controls the sittings, establishes what she could have read or been told, and concludes that she produces knowledge she has no ordinary way of holding. About the spirits who claim to speak through her he concludes nothing at all. To upset the law that all crows are black, he writes, it is enough to produce one white crow.
suggested_refs: The Piper sittings, the longest single investigation of James's psychical research career

stops.name: Plymouth: the school of applied ethics
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction on both counts: Encyclopedia.com attests the Plymouth school of applied ethics for 1891, but James's participation is reported rather than documented, and the month is a placeholder. Felix Adler's own journey file carries the same claim with the same hedge
stops.campa: Felix Adler convenes a summer school of applied ethics on the Massachusetts shore, and James is named among those who teach there, with John Dewey. Ministers and schoolteachers come for a season of pedagogy, economics and religion, and carry the vocabulary home with them in September. Nothing in the record traces a particular idea passing between the three men across those weeks. They were put in one room for a summer; all three spent the decade after it writing about what an education is for. Whether the room did any of that is not something the record can say.
suggested_refs: The Plymouth School of Applied Ethics, convened by Felix Adler from 1891

stops.name: London: president of the Society for Psychical Research
stops.date_confidence: corrected: the Society's own presidential succession puts James's term at 1894-95, after Arthur Balfour and before William Crookes. Wikipedia's William James article dates the presidency to 1884-85 and is wrong, conflating it with the founding of the American society, where he was a vice-president. James was not a founder of the London society, which Sidgwick, Myers and Barrett founded in 1882. The month is a placeholder
stops.campa: The London society elects him president for two years, an American in a chair held before him by Henry Sidgwick and by Arthur Balfour. Its most famous verdict is nine years old: Richard Hodgson's report on the Theosophical marvels at Adyar, which found them fraudulent and said so at length. Hodgson has since moved to Boston, where he now runs the Piper sittings for James. The same investigator, working the same way on a different woman, has arrived at the opposite conclusion and published that too.
suggested_refs: The Hodgson Report of 1885 on Helena Blavatsky, the Society's most notorious investigation before James's term
The Society for Psychical Research presidential succession, 1882-1900

stops.name: Chocorua: the farm under the mountain
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the acquisition of the Chocorua property is placed in the mid-1880s by the dossier and is not fixed to a month or day by any fetched source. The coordinate is Chocorua Lake, where the farm stood, rather than the point about four kilometres to the south-west that circulates in the dossier
stops.campa: He takes a summer property under Mount Chocorua in New Hampshire and the family keeps it for a quarter of a century. Of the two homes he ends with, this is the one not chosen for its nearness to a lecture hall. He writes in the mornings and walks the ridges in the afternoons, hard enough to strain the heart that will one day stop up here, and students come by train from Boston to argue on the porch. Alice runs the house through five children and a constant summer traffic of visitors.
suggested_refs: The James summer house at Chocorua, held from the mid-1880s until 1910

stops.name: 95 Irving Street, Cambridge: the house he meddled with
stops.date_confidence: corrected: the house was built in 1889 and the family moved in that autumn, not 1880 as the dossier has it; the month is approximate within the autumn. The dossier's description of the architect William Ralph Emerson as James's brother-in-law is false; Emerson was a cousin of Ralph Waldo Emerson and the house was an ordinary professional commission. The coordinate is Nominatim's William James House rather than the point 840 metres north-west that circulates
stops.campa: The house goes up in 1889 to a design by the architect William Ralph Emerson: three storeys, square, three chimneys, a gambrel roof, brown cedar shingles. Downstairs a library with bookcases to the ceiling, upstairs a small room where James writes standing at a desk. He interferes with the building so persistently that the contractor tells him he could save several thousand dollars by taking himself to Europe for the summer. Alice stays on here a decade after his death. Their children and grandchildren keep the house until 1968.
suggested_refs: The William James House, 95 Irving Street, Cambridge, built 1889
sources: news.harvard.edu/gazette, 'Storied Irving Street paves way to history' (2016)

stops.name: Harvard: The Principles of Psychology
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1890 for publication; the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: Two volumes, twelve years late, and the discipline has its first book in English that reads like literature and argues like physiology. The stream of thought; the self; the emotions taken as the body's own report on itself; and a chapter on habit that turns into the most quoted thing he ever wrote. He is given an endowed chair in psychology the year before it appears. Within five years he is telling correspondents that psychology bores him and that he means to spend what is left on philosophy.
stops.quote: Habit is thus the enormous fly-wheel of society, its most precious conservative agent.
stops.quote_source: The Principles of Psychology, vol. I (New York: Henry Holt, 1890), chapter IV, 'Habit'
suggested_refs: The Principles of Psychology, 2 vols., Henry Holt, 1890
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 57628, The Principles of Psychology vol. I

stops.name: Harvard: the degree Mary Whiton Calkins earned
stops.date_confidence: corrected: Calkins began studying with James in 1890 and was refused the doctorate in 1895, so the dossier's 1890 dating of the refusal is wrong. The month is a placeholder
stops.campa: Mary Whiton Calkins has studied with James since 1890, the year the Principles appeared. She sits the doctoral examination and the philosophy department recommends the degree unanimously. The president of the university, Charles William Eliot, who does not believe in degrees for women, refuses to grant it. Radcliffe offers her a substitute in 1902 and she declines that as well. James's verdict on the examination sits in the record beside Eliot's refusal, and has since 1895. The Harvard degree is never granted.
stops.quote: the most brilliant examination for the Ph.D. that we have had at Harvard
stops.quote_source: William James on Mary Whiton Calkins's doctoral examination, 1895, cited in Wikipedia, 'Mary Whiton Calkins'
suggested_refs: Mary Whiton Calkins's paired-associates method and her self-psychology, developed without a doctorate

stops.name: Yale, New Haven: the will to believe
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1896 for delivery to the Yale and Brown philosophical clubs; the month is a placeholder. The Yale coordinate stands for a lecture repeated at Providence, which is not given a separate stop here
stops.campa: Before the philosophical club at Yale, and again at Brown, he defends the right to believe ahead of the evidence, and he fences the right about tightly: only for options that are live, forced and momentous, and only where the evidence cannot settle the matter in time to act on it. Each of those words is a restriction. Critics read the title, drop the conditions, and take him to have licensed believing whatever is comforting. He denies it for the rest of his life, and the misreading outlives him by a century.
suggested_refs: 'The Will to Believe', delivered to the Yale and Brown philosophical clubs, 1896

stops.name: Boston: The Will to Believe between covers
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1897 for publication of the volume and of the Ingersoll lecture Human Immortality, on Britannica's bibliography; no fetched imprint page confirmed a month, so the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: The lecture comes out as a book with nine other popular essays. Among them is one delivered to young men who had written to ask him whether life was worth living, in a decade when suicide among students was lectured about openly and not obliquely. His answer is not an argument that it is worth living. It is an argument that the question stands open, that no proof either way is available in time, and that the conduct of the person asking is one of the things that will close it.
stops.quote: These, then, are my last words to you: Be not afraid of life. Believe that life is worth living, and your belief will help create the fact.
stops.quote_source: 'Is Life Worth Living?', in The Will to Believe and Other Essays in Popular Philosophy (New York: Longmans, Green, 1897)
suggested_refs: The Will to Believe and Other Essays in Popular Philosophy, Longmans Green, 1897
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 26659, The Will to Believe

stops.name: Berkeley: the word said out loud
stops.date_confidence: attested to 26 August 1898 for the address to the Philosophical Union. The coordinate is the campus rather than the downtown point about 1.3 kilometres west that circulates in the dossier
stops.campa: To the Philosophical Union at Berkeley he gives an address called Philosophical Conceptions and Practical Results, and in the course of it puts into print, for the first time anywhere, a word he refuses to claim: pragmatism. The method he draws out of it is a rule for ending arguments that cannot be ended otherwise, by asking what difference in anyone's experience the answer would make. The word is in print from that afternoon on. He credits it to Charles Peirce, who coined it in the Cambridge club of the early seventies and never published it.
suggested_refs: 'Philosophical Conceptions and Practical Results', Berkeley, 26 August 1898

stops.name: Boston: against the Philippine war
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Stanford Encyclopedia places James's involvement with the Anti-Imperialist League and his public opposition to the Philippine annexation in 1898-99 without a precise date; the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: The United States takes the Philippines and then fights the Filipinos who had expected independence from the same war, and James writes to the Boston papers about it in language he never uses in a lecture hall. The League he joins is full of Boston men of his father's generation. His argument is not that empire is inefficient. It is that the nation is doing to another people the exact thing it was founded by refusing to have done to itself, and that the word civilization is being used to cover the doing.
suggested_refs: The Anti-Imperialist League, founded at Boston in June 1898

stops.name: Edinburgh: the Gifford Lectures
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1901-02 for the two courses of Gifford Lectures, published in 1902; the month is a placeholder and the particular hall within the university is not confirmed by any fetched source
stops.campa: His heart is failing and he has been two years too ill to teach, so he builds the Gifford Lectures out of what can be read in bed: conversion narratives, mystics, the letters of the converted and the tormented, the documents of religion rather than its doctrines. On the first evening he rules the institutions out of court and takes as his subject what happens to a person alone. Edinburgh fills the hall for two seasons. The book has never been out of print since.
stops.quote: Religion, therefore, as I now ask you arbitrarily to take it, shall mean for us the feelings, acts, and experiences of individual men in their solitude, so far as they apprehend themselves to stand in relation to whatever they may consider the divine.
stops.quote_source: The Varieties of Religious Experience: A Study in Human Nature (New York: Longmans, Green, 1902), Lecture II, 'Circumscription of the Topic'
suggested_refs: The Gifford Lectures on Natural Theology, University of Edinburgh, 1901-02
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 621, The Varieties of Religious Experience

stops.name: Cambridge: does consciousness exist
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1904-05 for the composition of the essays later collected as Essays in Radical Empiricism; the month is a placeholder and the collection itself is posthumous
stops.campa: In a run of essays written in his sixties he takes apart the thing his own psychology had assumed. Does consciousness exist, he asks, and answers that it does not, not as a stuff or an entity: there is only experience, taken one way as a knower and another way as a thing known. And the relations between experiences are themselves experienced, felt as directly as the terms they join, so that no faculty has to be invented to supply them. It is the most technical work of his life and the least read. He does not live to assemble it into a book.
suggested_refs: Essays in Radical Empiricism, assembled posthumously in 1912

stops.name: Stanford: the moral equivalent of war
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the 1906 Stanford delivery of the address published in 1910 as 'The Moral Equivalent of War' is a dossier claim that no fetched source confirmed in this pass; the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: Teaching a term in California, he puts a proposal to a Stanford audience. The martial virtues are real, he says; pacifists lose the argument by pretending otherwise; and what is wanted is a conscription of the young into hard civilian labour, into mines and fisheries and foundries and the building of roads, so that the hardihood war produces can be produced without the war. He is not arguing for a substitute army. He is arguing that the thing war does to a population has to be done by something, and that the something is open to choice. The address is not printed until 1910.
suggested_refs: 'The Moral Equivalent of War', published 1910
sources: Dossier synthesis of the 1906 Stanford term; not independently confirmed

stops.name: Harvard: emeritus in January
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1907; the day is a placeholder
stops.campa: He resigns the chair in January, thirty-five years after the physiology instructorship, and is made professor emeritus. He has been trying to get out for a decade and has twice been talked back in. What he wants the remaining time for is a system: a metaphysics standing under the pragmatism and the radical empiricism together, argued through properly, between covers. He gets three and a half years. The unfinished manuscript is published after his death as Some Problems of Philosophy.
suggested_refs: Some Problems of Philosophy, the unfinished system, published 1911

stops.name: Boston: Pragmatism, and the roof comes off
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1907 for publication of the Lowell lectures as Pragmatism: A New Name for Some Old Ways of Thinking; the month is approximate
stops.campa: The Lowell lectures become a book and the book makes him famous outside the universities in a way no American philosopher has been before. He offers pragmatism as a method for settling otherwise interminable disputes by asking what difference in anybody's experience the answer would make. Then he turns the method on truth itself, and says that the true is the expedient in the way of our thinking, and the roof comes off. Critics on two continents read that as truth put up for sale. He spends the two years left explaining that expedient in the long run and on the whole is not the same thing as convenient this afternoon.
stops.quote: Pragmatism ... lies in the midst of our theories, like a corridor in a hotel. Innumerable chambers open out of it. In one you may find a man writing an atheistic volume; in the next someone on his knees praying for faith and strength; in a third a chemist investigating a body's properties.
stops.quote_source: Pragmatism: A New Name for Some Old Ways of Thinking (New York: Longmans, Green, 1907), Lecture II, 'What Pragmatism Means'; James credits the image to the Italian pragmatist Giovanni Papini
suggested_refs: The Meaning of Truth: A Sequel to 'Pragmatism' (1909), written to answer the critics

stops.name: Manchester College, Oxford: a pluralistic universe
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1908 for the Hibbert Lectures; the month is a placeholder. The venue was Manchester College, Oxford, now Harris Manchester College, whose Nominatim coordinate is used here; the dossier's bare 'Manchester' invites confusion with the city, and the generic central-Oxford point sits about 500 metres away
stops.campa: At Manchester College he argues against the Absolute for the length of eight lectures. The universe is not one thing thinking itself, he says; it is many things, genuinely many, connected in some directions and not in others, and unfinished, so that what happens next is not already contained in what has happened. He calls this a pluralistic universe and means the plural literally. Oxford, where absolute idealism is the house philosophy, listens to an American of sixty-six. The lectures appear as A Pluralistic Universe the following year.
suggested_refs: A Pluralistic Universe: Hibbert Lectures at Manchester College (1909)
sources: New England Historical Society, 'William James Founds Psychology in America'

stops.name: Clark University, Worcester: one day to see Freud
stops.date_confidence: attested for the conference and for the honorary doctorates of 10 September 1909. James's own presence, his walk with Jung and his remark to Freud are reported in the dossier and staged in Freud's and Jung's journey files; Clark University's own record does not name him. The coordinate is the pin those two files already use
stops.campa: Sigmund Freud has been brought to Worcester by G. Stanley Hall for the university's twentieth anniversary, to lecture on psychoanalysis, and Carl Jung has come with him. James, sixty-seven and unwell, travels down for a single day to see what Freud is like. He walks apart with Jung and talks about psychical research and about the varieties of religious experience. To Freud he says that the future of psychology belongs to work of this kind. Both visitors take honorary doctorates on the tenth. Then James goes home and writes to Geneva what he actually thinks.
suggested_refs: The Clark University twentieth-anniversary conference, September 1909, and the group photograph on the steps

stops.name: Chocorua: the letter to Flournoy
stops.date_confidence: attested: the letter is dated Chocorua, 28 September 1909, and is printed in The Letters of William James, vol. II
stops.campa: Eighteen days after Worcester he writes to Theodore Flournoy in Geneva, the one correspondent working the same borderland between psychology and religion that he works. The letter says both things at once, which is why it is the best evidence of what he thought: that Freud's ideas should be pushed to their utmost limits because they cannot fail to throw light on human nature, and that the man himself struck him as obsessed with fixed ideas. He is sixty-seven, and eleven months from his own death. Of the dream theory he uses the word dangerous.
stops.quote: I went there for one day in order to see what Freud was like, and met also Yung of Zurich... I hope that Freud and his pupils will push their ideas to their utmost limits, so that we may learn what they are. They can't fail to throw light on human nature; but I confess that he made on me personally the impression of a man obsessed with fixed ideas. I can make nothing in my own case with his dream theories, and obviously 'symbolism' is a most dangerous method.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Theodore Flournoy, Chocorua, 28 September 1909, in The Letters of William James, vol. II, ed. Henry James (Boston: Atlantic Monthly Press, 1920)
suggested_refs: The James-Flournoy correspondence on mediumship, subliminal selves and religious experience
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 38091, The Letters of William James vol. II

stops.name: Bad Nauheim: the cure that does nothing
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Wikipedia states only that James sailed to Europe in the spring of 1910 for experimental heart treatment that proved unsuccessful. The identification of the place as Bad Nauheim and of the treatment as the carbonated-bath regimen is dossier-only and is attested in no fetched source. The month is a placeholder
stops.campa: He crosses for the last time to take a cure. The carbonated springs of Bad Nauheim are the fashionable European treatment for a failing heart, prescribed as baths and as graduated walks up marked slopes, and men with his diagnosis come from everywhere to try them. On him the treatment does nothing. He is sixty-eight and knows what the pain means when it arrives on a flight of stairs. His brother Henry, ill himself, is in England, and William goes across to him.
suggested_refs: The Nauheim regimen of carbonated baths and graduated hill walks, standard cardiac treatment of the period
sources: dossier, final illness section; the Nauheim identification is not independently attested

stops.name: Chocorua: the twenty-sixth of August
stops.date_confidence: attested: he returned to America on 18 August 1910 and his heart failed on 26 August at the Chocorua house, aged sixty-eight
stops.campa: The brothers sail home together in August, Henry crossing to America with him. William reaches the New Hampshire farm on the eighteenth and dies there on the twenty-sixth, of heart failure, aged sixty-eight, twenty-five years after he first went looking for evidence that anything of a person survives. He had settled nothing about that, and had told friends he did not expect to. Alice is with him. The mountain stands behind the house and the summer is not over.
suggested_refs: The Chocorua house, held by the family from the mid-1880s to 1910

stops.name: Cambridge Cemetery: the family plot
stops.date_confidence: attested for burial in the James family plot at Cambridge Cemetery in August 1910; the exact day is a placeholder. Three different coordinates for this grave circulate in the working material and two of them fall inside Harvard Yard, two and a half kilometres east; the value used here is Nominatim's location for the cemetery itself
stops.campa: He is laid in the family plot at Cambridge Cemetery, beside his parents. Alice comes here in time, and Henry's ashes are brought back from England to lie with them. Two miles east, in 1963, the university raises a tower named for him, fifteen storeys of white concrete visible from most of Cambridge. In 1936 a radio broadcaster credits him with the claim that a man uses ten percent of his brain, a figure he never gave, and that sentence now travels further than anything he wrote.
suggested_refs: William James Hall, Harvard, built 1963 to Minoru Yamasaki's design
The ten-percent-of-the-brain misattribution, traced to Lowell Thomas in 1936
